title: Chapter 61 — Stubb Kills a Whale
paragraphs: If Starbuck saw the apparition of the Squid as an omen, Queequeg saw it as something else entirely.
"When you see him squid," said the savage, honing his harpoon in the bow of his hoisted boat, "then you quick see him sperm whale."

The next day was exceedingly still and sultry, and with nothing special to occupy them, the Pequod's crew could hardly resist the spell of sleep brought on by such an empty sea. For this part of the Indian Ocean through which we were then voyaging is not what whalemen call a lively ground; that is, it offers fewer glimpses of porpoises, dolphins, flying fish, and other lively inhabitants of busier waters than the grounds off the Rio de la Plata, or the in-shore ground off Peru.

It was my turn to stand watch at the foremast-head, and with my shoulders leaning against the slack royal shrouds, I swayed lazily back and forth in what felt like enchanted air. No resolve could hold out against it. Losing all awareness in that dreamy mood, my soul finally left my body, though my body went on swaying as a pendulum does long after the force that set it moving has been removed.

Before I lost myself completely, I had noticed that the men at the main and mizzen mastheads were already drowsy. So in the end all three of us hung swinging lifelessly from the spars, and for every swing we made, the dozing helmsman below gave a nod. The waves, too, nodded their lazy crests; and across the wide trance of the sea, east nodded to west, and the sun over all.

Suddenly bubbles seemed to burst under my closed eyelids; my hands clamped onto the shrouds like vises; some unseen, merciful power saved me; with a jolt I came back to life. And there! Close under our lee, not forty fathoms away, a gigantic Sperm Whale lay rolling in the water like the overturned hull of a frigate, his broad, glossy back, the hue of an Ethiopian's, shining in the sun like a mirror. As he rocked lazily in the trough of the sea, calmly spouting his misty jet every now and then, the whale looked like a stout burgher smoking his pipe on a warm afternoon. But that pipe, poor whale, was your last. As if touched by some magician's wand, the drowsy ship and every sleeper aboard sprang awake at once; and more than twenty voices from every part of the vessel, together with the three cries from aloft, raised the familiar shout, while the great fish slowly and steadily spouted the sparkling brine into the air.
"Clear away the boats! Luff!" cried Ahab. And obeying his own order, he slammed the helm down before the helmsman could reach the spokes.

The crew's sudden shouts must have alarmed the whale, because before the boats were down he turned majestically and swam off to leeward — yet so steadily and calmly, raising so few ripples, that Ahab, thinking he might not be alarmed yet after all, ordered that no oar be used and that nobody speak above a whisper. So, sitting on the gunwales like Ontario Indians, we paddled along swiftly but silently; the calm made it impossible to set the noiseless sails. Soon, as we glided after him like this, the monster flipped his tail straight up forty feet into the air and then sank out of sight like a tower swallowed up.

"There go flukes!" was the cry — an announcement immediately followed by Stubb's producing his match and lighting his pipe, for now a breathing space was granted. After the full interval of his sounding (his deep dive) had passed, the whale rose again, and being now ahead of the smoker's boat, and much nearer to it than to any of the others, Stubb counted on the honor of the capture. It was obvious now that the whale had at last become aware of his pursuers. All cautious silence was therefore no longer of any use. Paddles were dropped, and oars came loudly into play. And still puffing at his pipe, Stubb cheered his crew on to the attack.
Yes, a mighty change had come over the fish. Fully alive to his danger, he was going "head out," his head projecting at a slant from the mad yeast he was brewing.*

*It will be seen elsewhere what a very light substance the entire interior of the sperm whale's enormous head consists of. Though apparently the most massive, it is by far the most buoyant part of him. So he raises it into the air with ease, and invariably does so when going at his utmost speed. Besides, such is the breadth of the upper part of the front of his head, and such the tapering, cutwater shape of the lower part, that by raising his head at a slant he may be said to transform himself from a bluff-bowed, sluggish galliot (a broad Dutch cargo boat) into a sharp-pointed New York pilot-boat.

"Start her, start her, my men! Don't hurry yourselves — take plenty of time — but start her; start her like thunderclaps, that's all," cried Stubb, sputtering out smoke as he spoke. "Start her, now; give them the long and strong stroke, Tashtego. Start her, Tash, my boy — start her, all; but keep cool, keep cool — cucumbers is the word — easy, easy — only start her like grim death and grinning devils, and raise the buried dead straight up out of their graves, boys — that's all. Start her!"

"Woo-hoo! Wa-hee!" screamed the Gay Header in reply, raising some old war-whoop to the skies, as every oarsman in the straining boat involuntarily lurched forward with the one tremendous leading stroke the eager Indian gave.
But his wild screams were answered by others equally wild. "Kee-hee! Kee-hee!" yelled Daggoo, straining forward and backward on his seat like a pacing tiger in his cage.

"Ka-la! Koo-loo!" howled Queequeg, as if smacking his lips over a mouthful of grenadier's steak. And so with oars and yells the keels cut the sea. Meanwhile, Stubb, keeping his place in the lead, still urged his men on to the attack, all the while puffing smoke from his mouth. Like desperadoes they tugged and strained, until the welcome cry was heard — "Stand up, Tashtego! — give it to him!" The harpoon was hurled. "Stern all!" The oarsmen backed water; at the same moment something went hot and hissing along every one of their wrists. It was the magical line. An instant before, Stubb had swiftly taken two extra turns with it around the loggerhead (the post in the stern around which the line is snubbed), from which, because of its increasingly rapid circling, a blue smoke of hemp now jetted up and mingled with the steady fumes from his pipe. As the line passed round and round the loggerhead, so also, just before reaching that point, it passed blisteringly through and through both of Stubb's hands, from which the hand-cloths — squares of quilted canvas sometimes worn at such times — had accidentally dropped. It was like holding an enemy's sharp two-edged sword by the blade, with that enemy all the time struggling to wrench it out of your grip.

"Wet the line! Wet the line!" cried Stubb to the tub oarsman (the one seated by the tub), who, snatching off his hat, dashed seawater into it.* More turns were taken, so that the line began to hold its place. The boat now flew through the boiling water like a shark all fins. Stubb and Tashtego here changed places — stem for stern — a staggering business indeed in that rocking commotion.

*Partly to show how indispensable this act is, it may be stated here that in the old Dutch fishery a mop was used to dash the running line with water; in many other ships, a wooden piggin, or bailer, is set aside for that purpose. Your hat, however, is the most convenient.

From the vibrating line stretching the entire length of the upper part of the boat, and from its now being tighter than a harpstring, you would have thought the craft had two keels — one cleaving the water, the other the air — as the boat churned on through both opposing elements at once. A continual cascade played at the bows; a ceaseless whirling eddy in her wake; and at the slightest motion from within, even of just a little finger, the vibrating, cracking craft tipped her spasmodic gunwale over into the sea. So they rushed on, each man clinging to his seat with all his might to keep from being tossed into the foam, and the tall form of Tashtego at the steering oar crouching almost double to bring down his center of gravity. Whole Atlantics and Pacifics seemed to pass as they shot on their way, until at last the whale somewhat slackened his flight.

"Haul in — haul in!" cried Stubb to the bowsman; and, facing round toward the whale, all hands began pulling the boat up to him while the boat was still being towed along. Soon drawing up alongside his flank, Stubb, firmly planting his knee in the clumsy cleat, darted dart after dart into the fleeing fish; at the word of command, the boat alternately backed away out of reach of the whale's horrible wallowing, and then drew up again for another throw.

Now the red tide poured from every side of the monster like brooks running downhill. His tortured body rolled not in brine but in blood, which bubbled and seethed for furlongs in their wake. The slanting sun, playing over this crimson pond in the sea, threw its reflection back into every face, so that the men all glowed at one another like red men. And all the while the whale's spout-hole shot out jet after jet of white smoke in agony, and the excited headsman's mouth shot out puff after furious puff; for after every dart Stubb hauled in his bent lance (by the line tied to it), straightened it again and again with a few quick blows against the gunwale, and then drove it into the whale again and again.

"Pull up — pull up!" he now cried to the bowsman, as the waning whale slackened in his wrath. "Pull up! — close to!" And the boat drew up along the fish's flank. Then, reaching far over the bow, Stubb slowly churned his long sharp lance into the fish, and kept it there, carefully churning and churning, as if cautiously feeling for some gold watch that the whale might have swallowed, and which he was afraid of breaking before he could hook it out. But that gold watch he sought was the innermost life of the fish. And now it is struck; for, starting from his trance into that unspeakable thing called his "flurry," the monster wallowed horribly in his blood and wrapped himself in impenetrable, mad, boiling spray, so that the endangered boat, instantly dropping astern, had a hard time struggling blindly out of that frenzied twilight into the clear air of the day.

And now, his flurry subsiding, the whale once more rolled into view, surging from side to side, spasmodically expanding and contracting his spout-hole with sharp, cracking, agonized breaths. At last, gush after gush of clotted red gore, as if it were the purple dregs of red wine, shot into the frightened air, and falling back again, ran dripping down his motionless flanks into the sea. His heart had burst!
"He's dead, Mr. Stubb," said Daggoo.
"Yes — both pipes smoked out!" And withdrawing his own pipe from his mouth, Stubb scattered the dead ashes over the water, and for a moment stood thoughtfully eyeing the vast corpse he had made.
